t: the zavah. A woman who sees blood during the days of her zivah, which defiles her in such a way that she is obligated to bring an offering after she becomes pure (see below, halachah 6).
and the woman who gave birth. After the days of her impurity and the days of her purity are complete, she is obligated to bring an offering (below, halachah 5).
and the zav. A man from whom a discharge flows that defiles him in such a way that he is obligated to bring an offering after he becomes pure (as detailed below in chapter 2).
and the metzora. After he is healed of his tzara'at and becomes pure he is obligated to bring an offering (as detailed below in chapter 4).
even though he became pure of his impurity, immersed, and the sun set. He waited until evening after his immersion, and now he is pure even for eating terumah (see Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:2).

he is forbidden to eat sacrificial food. And if he touched sacrificial food he disqualified it, by the law of a tevul yom touching it (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:3-4, 11:4). And he is also forbidden to enter the Temple from the Israelites' courtyard inward (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:7).
as we explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 18:14.

a convert who circumcised and immersed and has not yet brought his offering. A person who comes to convert is obligated in circumcision, immersion and bringing an offering (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:1-5).

and for this reason he does not eat sacrificial food, since he has not yet become like the fit of Israel. The reason he is forbidden sacrificial food is not that he lacks the atonement of the offering, but that he is not considered a full Israelite until he brings his offering.
brought one bird. One of the two birds that the convert must bring.

eats sacrificial food in the evening. Even though his whole offering has not yet been offered, since one bird suffices to permit him to eat sacrificial food (but before evening arrives he is forbidden, lest the priests did not offer the bird he brought until close to evening; Tosafot, Chagigah 21a, and see below, halachah 12).
as we explained in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. 1:6.
and if her means do not suffice. That she is poor (compare Hilchot Shegagot 10:2).
she brings a nest. Two birds.

a woman who gave birth does not bring her offering on the fortieth day for a male or on the eightieth day for a female, etc.. A woman who gave birth is impure from the time of birth for seven days for a male and fourteen for a female, and has the law of a niddah. After these days she immerses, and the days after that until the fortieth day after the birth of a male and the eightieth day after the birth of a female are called "days of purity," and any blood she sees in them does not defile her (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 4:5, Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 5:2). After immersion and during her days of purity the woman who gave birth is impure like a tevulat yom and is forbidden to eat terumah and sacrificial food until her sun sets at the end of the fortieth day for a male and the eightieth for a female, and then she is permitted terumah, but is still forbidden sacrificial food until she brings her offering the next day (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 5:4).

and it is the day about which it is said: "and when the days of her purification are completed". For the word "u'milot" here means after they have been completed, and on the fortieth and eightieth day they are not yet completed (Rabbeinu Yitzchak, Riko"v).
within the completion. Within forty days for a male or eighty for a female.
she has not fulfilled her obligation. And she must bring another offering to permit her sacrificial food.

even if she brought for the earlier births within the days of completion of this birth. Although the days of completion of the earlier births have passed, she does not fulfill her obligation with this offering until she brings it after the days of completion of the last birth have ended (see below, halachah 8).

but the olah and the asham do not hold back. Although they must complete the offerings for which they are obligated, the completion of purity with regard to eating sacrificial food does not depend on them but on bringing the chatat (see also Hilchot Nezirut 10:8).
we have already explained in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. 14:10.
on their behalf. For them.
for a person brings an offering for his children, etc.. Hilchot Shegagot 10:6.
for his minor sons and daughters. Even though they have no understanding, from which we learn that the owner's awareness is not required (and see below 3:6).
not at the time of her niddah. Not during the days when she becomes a niddah but during the days when she becomes a zavah.
and this is a major zavah, etc.. Unlike a minor zavah whose blood flowed only one or two days, who does not count seven but keeps only one day for her purification and is exempt from the offering.
and we have already explained the matter of the niddah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah, chapter 6.
for we have already explained. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 7:10.
and there we explained. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah, chapter 10.
whose pregnancy was not established. She was not presumed to be pregnant.

this is a doubtful woman who gave birth. But where she was presumed pregnant, even if she did not know what she miscarried she is presumed to have miscarried a fetus and her chatat is eaten (Kesef Mishneh, and see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:19).

and this chatat turns out to be unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. For since she is not obligated, her offering is not considered sacred but unconsecrated animals, which it is forbidden to slaughter in the courtyard.
for they are forbidden for benefit. And all the more so for eating.
as we explained in Hilchot Shechitah. 2:2.
she brings even for the second. And she does not fulfill her obligation with only one offering.
she gave birth to a female. For whom the days of completion are eighty days.
and she brings only one offering. After the days of completion of the last miscarriage have passed.

she miscarried a fetus on the night of the eighty-first ... she brings for it on its own. For the night before the eighty-first day is already considered after the completion for this purpose (see below 3:4).
any fetus she miscarries within the eighty of this second female, she is exempt for it. She need not bring a separate offering for it.
tumtum. Whose sexual organs are covered and whose sex is unclear. [Note: the Rambam in the Commentary on the Mishnah vocalizes this word differently.]

androgynos. One who has both male and female organs; each one of them is in doubt whether it is male or female (Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25, and see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:18 on the law of the impurity of a woman who gave birth to them).
perhaps the first was a male. For the days of completion of a male are only forty days.
doubtful five births or five discharges. It is not known whether she is obligated in an offering for them.

she brings one offering and eats sacrificial food, and the rest are not an obligation on her. For in order to permit her to eat sacrificial food it suffices to bring one offering, and she is not obligated to bring the rest since her obligation is in doubt.

she brings one offering and eats sacrificial food, and the rest are an obligation on her. For although she is certainly obligated in five offerings, she is permitted to eat sacrificial food already after she brought the first offering.

she brings two offerings, etc.. Although it would seem that one offering suffices to permit her to eat sacrificial food, the Sages decreed that where she is obligated both for certain and for doubtful ones she must bring two offerings, one for the certain and one for the doubtful (for the reason for the decree see Aruch HaShulchan 232:10, Sefat Emet Keritot 8a, and see Piskei VeShitot).
if before she converted she gave birth. And she is exempt from the offering of one who gave birth, since she gave birth while a gentile.
we have already explained in Hilchot Shegagot. 3:11.

that all those lacking atonement through doubt ... are obligated to bring after Yom Kippur, etc.. Although Yom Kippur atones in cases of doubtful transgression and exempts from bringing an asham taluy (see ibid., halachah 9), it does not exempt these offerings, which come to complete purity so as to permit eating sacrificial food.
she brings the money of the nests and puts it in the shofar. She puts the money she brought for the nests she owes into a chest (shofar) in the Temple designated for this.
and eats sacrificial food in the evening. For she can rely on the priests having offered her offering that day.
for the court of priests does not rise from there. From their seat in the Temple.
as we explained in Shekalim. 2:2.
and in Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash VeHa'ovdim Bo. 7:9.

a woman who brought her chatat and died, etc.. But if she brought her olah and died, her heirs do not bring her chatat (Mishnah Kinnim 2:5), since it is a chatat whose owners died, whose law is that it must die (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1). This law applies also to a man, such as a zav or metzora, who are obligated to bring a chatat and an olah (Ramban and Meiri, Kiddushin 13b; Raavad, Kinnim 2:5).
while alive. While she was alive.

her property was already mortgaged for the offering, and the lien is by Torah law. For since the woman was obligated in an offering, her property was mortgaged for it, and this lien rests on the property even after her death, even if the woman did not actually set aside the olah.
semen that comes from a disease of the organs in which it gathers. As a result of a disease in the sexual organs.
drawn out and descending like the water of barley dough. Like a dough made from barley flour that does not stick well but tends to crumble.
faint like the white of a spoiled egg. A thin fluid whose color is faint (inclining slightly to red - Commentary on the Mishnah, Zavim 2:2), like the white of a spoiled egg.
tied. Sticky and viscous.
one who sees the discharge of zivah that causes him to be a zav, etc.. A sighting that turns him from a ba'al keri into a zav, which is the second sighting (see below, halachah 5, and see Riko"v).
because of illness or compulsion and the like. That he saw a discharge that does not stem from a disease of the reproductive organs but from other systems of the body or other influences.

because of his flesh. The weakness of his reproductive organs (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zavim 2:2; unlike a ba'al keri, who is impure even when the emission came not because of his flesh, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 5:1).
they examine the zav. They check that the discharge he saw does not come from other causes.
gross eating. Heavy eating that weighs on the body.
foods or drinks that lead to emission of semen. For example, eggs and hot milk (see Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:6).
or he carried a heavy load or jumped from place to place, etc.. For these things weaken the body's strength and burden it, and can lead to seeing a discharge (Commentary on the Mishnah ibid.).
from time to time. Twenty-four hours.
it is from semen. And not from a disease of the reproductive organs.
as long as he is in distress. As long as the sighting can be attributed to the distress caused by them and not to his flesh.

and he converted, he is defiled with zivah immediately, etc.. For example, if he was circumcised before the conversion; otherwise, we attribute it to the circumcision as long as he is in distress (Tosefta Zavim 2:7).

and we do not attribute it to him from time to time. Since after his conversion he is considered a newborn minor, we pay no attention to the emission he saw before he converted (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zavim 2:3).
a minor. Even a one-day-old defiles through zivah (below 3:6).
if he was nursing from her or needed his mother. That he is in distress when she is ill or he catches it from her, so that he could see a discharge as a result.
as will be explained. Below, halachah 6.

in order to count three sightings with it to obligate him to an offering. Although with regard to impurity he is considered a zav even when the first sighting was due to compulsion, with regard to the obligation of an offering he is not liable until he sees the first two sightings because of his flesh.
since he has become subject to impurity. For after he saw two sightings he became a zav and was established as one who sees zivah.
he is like a ba'al keri. That he is a first-degree source of impurity, and becomes pure through immersion in a mikveh and nightfall.
this is a zav. Who is a primary source of impurity that defiles a bed and a seat (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:1-2).

he needs a count of seven and immersion in living water. He must count seven days clean of discharge and on the seventh immerse in a spring whose waters are living (flowing, unlike a mikveh; see Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:5, 9:8).
but only an offering. But with regard to impurity the two are equal (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav ibid.).

because Scripture made the zavah depend on days, etc.. The zavah's impurity depends on her seeing blood on three consecutive days (above 1:6, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:7), whether she saw once each day or many times. Not so the zav, whose impurity depends on the number of sightings he saw, whether he saw them in one day or on three consecutive days.
a complete day. A full day that begins at night and ends on the following night.
needless to say, if he saw one at night and a second by day, that they combine. For in this case both sightings were in the same day itself.
the time of immersion and drying. The time it takes him to immerse and dry off.
this counts as two sightings. It is counted as two sightings.
even if the discharge stopped in between, it is one sighting. For the sightings are not separated from one another by less than the time of immersion and drying.
for the days divide the sighting. Since there is a division here between two days, the sighting is also divided in two even when it does not have the measure of two sightings.
twilight. The time of dusk, when it is doubtful whether it belongs to the previous day or to the night of the following day (and its exact time is explained in Hilchot Shabbat 5:4).
this is in doubt regarding impurity. Perhaps he saw part of it at the end of the day and part at the beginning of the night, in which case he is impure as a zav who saw two sightings.

and in doubt regarding an offering. Perhaps the second sighting was partly at the end of the day and partly at the beginning of the night, in which case it is divided in two, and he is a zav who saw three sightings and is obligated in an offering.
counts seven clean days like a zavah. He counts seven days clean of discharge, just as the zavah counts seven days clean of blood (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:11).
and immerses on the seventh. During the day.
and waits for nightfall. He waits until evening.
cancels everything. The entire count is void.
even at the end of the seventh day after he immersed. Before night arrived (but a sighting on the eighth night does not cancel, as below, halachah 4).
and begins to count seven clean days from after the day of the last sighting. For the clean days must be consecutive, without discharge.
cancels only his day. For the day on which he saw an emission is not counted in the count of seven, but it does not cancel the seven clean days.
counts three days after it. In order to complete the four days he had already counted to the count of seven.
on the first day of the days of the count. Of the seven clean days.
he is presumed pure. For he was initially presumed pure, and this presumption was not canceled, since at the end it was found to be so (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:21-22).
as we explained. Above, halachah 1.

even if he saw three sightings at the end of the seventh day of the seven clean days. Although the seven clean days are nearly over, the sightings still count toward canceling and not toward an offering.
a zav who saw two sightings. Who does not bring an offering and whose purification ends at the end of the seven clean days.
although the last three do not cancel. And he must count seven new clean days for the second three sightings since there is a new zivah here (see Tosefta Zavim 1:9).

for he did not go out at a time fit for an offering, and the night is a time lacking for everything. Since the zav can bring his offering only on the eighth day and not on the night before it (for the night is considered a time unfit for all offerings), it turns out that the zav never had any time at which he could offer his first offering, and therefore the sightings of this night do not obligate him in an additional offering.

except for a woman who gave birth who miscarried on the eighty-first night. For a woman who gave birth to a female brings her offering on the eighty-first day after birth (above 1:5), and if she miscarried a fetus on the night before, she is obligated in an additional offering for it, although the time of the first offering had not yet arrived to be offered.
as we explained. Above 1:8.
from the tradition. A halachic tradition.

and he brings a second offering for this last zivah, for the first sighting ... is regarded as semen. For it defiles him only as a ba'al keri, and he does not become a zav until he sees a second sighting (above 2:5-6). Therefore we follow the sightings that occurred on the eighth day, at a time fit for an offering, and he must bring an additional offering.
even a one-day-old minor, and converts and slaves. See also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:4.
and it seems to me that atonement is brought for them. For the deaf-mute and the mentally incompetent (for slaves, atonement is certainly brought, see Hilchot Shegagot 10:6).
for they are like a minor without understanding. And for a minor atonement is brought to let him eat sacrificial food (above 1:5).
a eunuch by man and a eunuch by nature. A person whose sexual development is impaired, whether it was impaired by human hands or he was born impaired (see Hilchot Ishut 2:13-14).
are defiled by zivah like all people. See also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:5.
the tumtum and the androgynos. See above 1:9.
we apply to them the stringencies of a man and the stringencies of a woman. Since it is in doubt whether they are a man or a woman (see Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25).

are defiled by blood like women and by white discharge like men. If they see blood they become a niddah or zavah like a woman who sees blood, and if they see a discharge or emission they are defiled by it like men (see also Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 1:6-7).
bring an offering and it is not eaten. By the law of the offering of one lacking atonement who comes on a doubt (see above 1:6).
the red. Blood.

this does not cancel. For although they are defiled by white and by red, neither one cancels the seven clean days of the other, since whether they are male or female they never cancel in this way (see Kesef Mishneh).
after they purify him with cedar wood and hyssop, etc.. As detailed in Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at, chapter 11.
after all this he may enter Jerusalem. For until now he was forbidden to enter Jerusalem (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:1-2).
and he is a tevul yom. Who is a second-degree impurity (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 10:2).
and waits for nightfall. He waits until evening, and then he is pure even for terumah (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 11:2).
in the days of his being confirmed. In the days when he was a confirmed metzora.
in the Women's Courtyard, in the Chamber of the Metzoraim, where. See Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:7-8.
even though he did not put it out of his mind. And he guarded himself from becoming defiled.
as we explained. Above, halachah 1.
the metzora stands outside the Israelites' Courtyard. For he is forbidden to enter the Israelites' Courtyard as long as he lacks atonement (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:7).
opposite the eastern gate, facing west. He stands opposite the eastern gate of the courtyard (the Nicanor Gate) facing west toward the Sanctuary.
and there they give the sotot to drink. See Hilchot Sotah 3:3-4.
with the log of oil. That the metzora brings together with his offerings (Leviticus 14:10).
in the east. In the eastern part of the courtyard.
like all wave offerings. All of which are done in the east (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:6).

and he puts both his hands into the courtyard and leans on it. Although it is forbidden for an impure person to put his hands into the Temple, this is not a Torah prohibition (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:18), and in this case they did not forbid it since the leaning must be done only in the courtyard and by the owners (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:8, 3:11).

and they slaughter it immediately. There, near the eastern gate, since the slaughter must be done in the place of the leaning and immediately after it (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:12). And this place is fit for slaughtering the most holy offerings because it is called "north" (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:15-16).

one in his right hand, and he pours into his left hand and sprinkles with his right finger. He receives the blood in his right hand and transfers it to his left hand, so that he can afterward sprinkle the blood with his right finger on the metzora, as below.
carries it and throws it on the altar. In the way the blood of the other asham offerings is thrown (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:2).
from the inside. From within the courtyard.
and the metzora puts in his head, etc.. For if the blood were taken outside the courtyard the offering would be disqualified (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:35).
on the cartilage of his right ear. As explained below 5:1.
and he shall put on the thumb of his hand. On the thumb.
and pours. And he pours.
and the rest of the log is divided among the priests. For it is one of the priestly gifts (see Hilchot Bikkurim 1:4).
like the rest of the most holy offerings. Which are eaten only by male priests and in the courtyard (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:3).

for it is compared to the asham. The oil is equated to the asham in the verse (Leviticus 14:12; see Rashi, Zevachim 44b), and therefore it is considered an offering for several purposes (and see also Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:4).
the seven sprinklings and the placing on the thumbs. Sprinkling the oil seven times toward the Sanctuary, and putting it on the lobe and thumbs of the metzora (as above, halachah 2).

like one who eats sacrificial food before the throwing. Like a person who eats from the offerings before their blood was thrown on the altar, who is liable to lashes (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:4).
what is the lobe of the ear. The one mentioned in the atonement of the metzora (Leviticus 14:14, above 4:2).
this is the middle ridge. The protruding cartilage near the opening of the ear (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nega'im 14:9), and not the part called the earlobe today.
the sides of the thumbs. And not on the back of the thumb where the nail is.
the sides of their sides. The inner part of the thumb.
on the place of the blood of the asham. This implies on the place where the blood of the asham was put, even though the blood of the asham itself is no longer there.
that he slaughtered it not for its own sake. Not for the sake of an asham offering.

and it requires libations like the libations of the metzora's asham. For with every asham of a metzora one brings libations (for their details see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:6), and the same applies in these cases (and for the reason see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:17).

and the metzora needs another asham to qualify him. For although the offering is valid and is offered with its libations like any asham of a metzora, it does not qualify the metzora to eat sacrificial food unless it is done for his sake and properly.
he put his chatat before his asham. He slaughtered the chatat before the asham, out of order, for the asham of a metzora comes before his chatat (above 4:2, Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 9:8).

no one else may stir its blood. There is no benefit to this chatat even in having another priest stir its blood in the meantime (so that it does not congeal) until after the asham is offered, in order to offer it in order (although in similar cases one may do so, see Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 9:2-4, Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:4).
its form shall pass and it shall go out to the place of burning. They wait until it spoils and then burn it in the place where they burned disqualified sacrificial food.
a person may. He is permitted.
and his log. His log of oil.
after ten days. Just as libations may be brought a long time after their offering was brought (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 2:12).

and if he wanted to change the log to another metzora's asham, he may change it even though he sanctified it in a vessel. It is permitted to use the log of oil designated for this metzora's asham for another metzora's asham, even after it was placed in a sacred vessel.
before he poured. The priest on his palm (as above 4:2).
he shall fill it. He brings oil from his home and fills the log that is lacking, like a meal offering that became lacking before the kemitzah (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:16).

and he begins from the outset with the thumbs. Since he already finished the seven sprinklings, he may begin directly with the thumbs, since they are two separate acts (Rashi, Yoma 61a; similar to the sprinklings of the blood of the bull and the goat on Yom Kippur, Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 5:5-8).

as it says: "and the remainder of the oil," etc.. This implies that the placing on the head holds back only where some of the oil remains (as above 4:2), but where none remains, such as when the oil spilled or ran out, it does not hold back (Riko"v, and see there for other explanations).

he fills the log with oil. What he lacked in the placings, and he need not bring other oil as at the beginning (and although above, halachah 4, it says that when the oil was lacking after the pouring he must bring new oil, that is only when the oil was lacking from the log and not when it was lacking from the priest's palm - Rash, Nega'im 14:10, cited in Riko"v).

the gifts were not accepted, yet the leper became fit. Even though the gifts were not accepted, the leper became fit to eat of the sacred offerings. The later authorities disagree about the significance of the gifts not having been accepted (see Even HaAzel on this halakhah, Minchat Chinukh 176:2, Arukh HaShulchan 237:6).
a leper who was afflicted after he brought his guilt offering. Even if he had not yet had time to bring his other offerings.
he needs another offering for the second leprosy. Since from the time he brought his guilt offering he left the status of the first leprosy, he does not fulfill his obligation with a single offering.
and he brought his birds. Together with the other items he brings for his purification after being healed of leprosy (above 4:1).

one offering for all of them. Even though he was healed in the interim, since he had not yet managed to bring his guilt offering, it is considered one long leprosy, and therefore he fulfills his obligation with one offering (Rashi, Keritot 9b).

a poor person's offering. A poor leper brings a lamb for a guilt offering and two birds, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering, in place of the three sheep the rich person brings (above 1:3).

and afterwards one of the lepers died. And now the blood of the second sin offering cannot be sprinkled, lest it belong to the leper who died, and a sin offering whose owner died is left to die and is not offered on the altar (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1).
perhaps the one whose blood was sprinkled was his sin offering. And since his sin offering was already offered, he cannot bring another sin offering.
and one does not bring a sin offering of an animal on account of doubt. Ibid. 7:10.

for a rich person who brought a poor person's offering has not fulfilled his obligation. And since the bird sin offering is a poor person's offering, a rich person cannot bring it even as a doubtful offering (see ibid.).
let him write all his property to another and be found poor. Let him write a deed of gift of all his property to another person, and thereby become poor.
as we have explained. Above 1:6-7.
for the vower's means suffice. For the one who vowed is wealthy.

for this vower is obligated to bring the offerings of a rich person. And he does not fulfill his obligation with a poor person's offering (above 5:10; see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:9 and the commentary there).
